weaknesses: The central novelty claim is unsupported. For fixed D, enumerating arrangement cells or hyperplanes induced by D-point subsets is a classical computational-geometry approach; the proposed method largely implements this enumeration. Moreover, O(N^D) is not polynomial in the joint input size when D varies and therefore does not resolve the cited NP-hard problem.

The claimed O(N^D) runtime does not match the presented algorithm. At iteration i it retains Θ(i^D) configurations, so the fold alone performs Θ(N^(D+1)) configuration updates in the worst case. Candidate creation also evaluates a hyperplane on the preceding data, and repeated list appends can add further cost. No complexity proof or runtime measurements are supplied.

The implementation optimizes a different objective from Equation (1). Selected points lie exactly on the constructed hyperplane and receive prediction 0, but loss01 declares every zero prediction to have zero loss even though labels are ±1 and Equation (1) counts sign(w^T x)=0 as an error. The algorithm returns this boundary hyperplane without constructing the required perturbation into an adjacent cell, so its returned parameter need not solve Equation (2).

The correctness proof has fundamental gaps. Lemma 5 states a lower bound of D but proves only d, assumes the true label vector equals a realizable cell sign vector despite focusing on nonseparable data, and the theorem incorrectly infers that greater Hamming distance from an optimal cell implies greater loss relative to the true labels. These issues invalidate the claimed proof of exactness.

The stated general-position condition is insufficient for the code: fitw requires every selected raw D-by-D coordinate matrix to be invertible. For example, distinct points (1,0) and (2,0) are permitted by the affine general-position definition but form a singular matrix. Degenerate, duplicated, or collinear data are not handled, yet no evidence establishes that the UCI datasets satisfy the assumptions.

The use of Double arithmetic, an arbitrary 1e-8 threshold, exact comparisons to zero, and Gaussian elimination without robust pivoting is incompatible with a claim of provable exactness. Singular systems can also make rotatePivot fail to terminate. The stated sdp type signature uses independent type variables that must coincide and does not type-check as written.

The evaluation is inadequate for the main claims: it reports only training errors on five small, low-dimensional datasets, for which lower 0-1 training loss is tautological when ICE directly optimizes that objective. There are no timing or scaling results, memory measurements, exact-solver or arrangement-enumeration baselines, test-set results, optimality checks, ablations, or sufficient preprocessing and hyperparameter details. Consequently, neither efficiency, practical utility, reproducibility, nor the high-stakes prediction claims are supported.
